episode_title: Meta’s Muse: How we launched the most successful consumer product this year | Mona Sarantakos
description_html:
Muse is the #1 app in the App Store and arguably the fastest-growing AI consumer product of all time. Mona Sarantakos has led product on it since day one. She’s VP of Product at Meta Superintelligence Labs and a 10-year Meta veteran with over 20 years of experience as a PM. This is her first podcast interview.

We discuss:

1. How a weekend with OpenClaw on a Raspberry Pi turned into Muse

2. Why Muse waited seven months to launch, despite getting started before most of its competitors

3. How Nat Friedman, Alex Wang, and Mark Zuckerberg each left their imprint on the product

4. How the team uses “agent swarms” to surface user insights at scale

5. The use case nobody on the team predicted

6. How Jolly, a placeholder avatar, became an icon

7. The two levers that actually move activation for an AI agent

8. The #1 thing Mona looks for in PMs today

—

summary.overview: Mona Sarantakos, VP of Product at Meta Super Intelligence Labs and head of product for Muse, explains how the product grew from a small experiment inspired by OpenClaw into a rapidly growing consumer AI assistant. She discusses the team’s emphasis on trust, safety, personality, user feedback, product taste, and the still-evolving vision of agents that operate across everyday life rather than inside a single app.

takeaways.heading: The origin of Muse
takeaways.detail: Muse began after Nat Friedman urged a few Meta employees to try OpenClaw in early 2026. Mona spent a weekend connecting it to her email, calendar, and home automation, then experienced its automatically generated family and school-week summary as a glimpse of personal superintelligence.

takeaways.heading: From experiment to product
takeaways.detail: The initial group did not start with a formal project or product brief. They first experimented with the concept, then realized a consumer version would need to be safer, easier to set up, scalable, and substantially different from the original OpenClaw experience.

takeaways.heading: Why launch took seven months
takeaways.detail: The team spent much of the time establishing its own bar for reliability, safety, and security, especially as features such as browser access introduced new risks. Internal employees and external alpha testers expanded gradually, giving the team more confidence before launch.

takeaways.heading: Trust and safety
takeaways.detail: Mona repeatedly described the internal principle as “trust is a must”: if users encounter serious problems early, they will not trust the agent and will not use it. Muse developed extensive evals for prompt injection, harm, general safety, capabilities, behavior, and priority use cases.

takeaways.heading: Leadership and autonomy
takeaways.detail: Nat Friedman was deeply involved in architecture and security decisions, Alex Wang connected model research to product needs and pushed the team to launch, and Mark Zuckerberg shaped the product’s focus on helping people achieve goals rather than merely completing tasks. The small team retained substantial autonomy over many decisions.

takeaways.heading: Jolly’s role
takeaways.detail: Jolly began as a temporary creature in Alex Cornell’s prototype, but survived repeated attempts to replace it with a corporate logo. Mona said a personal agent should not feel like a corporate entity, and that the avatar helped make Muse feel like it belonged to the user.

takeaways.heading: Use cases and shopping
takeaways.detail: The team expected productivity, health, personal finance, and home automation to dominate, but shopping emerged as a major use case through dogfooding. Mona said agents should reduce decision paralysis without eliminating the browsing and inspiration people enjoy.

takeaways.heading: Agent swarms
takeaways.detail: Agent swarms analyzed conversations, product data, feedback, and synthetic data to identify patterns and produce detailed reports. They helped the team understand long-running, multi-turn consumer tasks that were not well represented in existing datasets or dashboards.

takeaways.heading: Activation and onboarding
takeaways.detail: Mona said word of mouth is the strongest activation mechanism because people understand Muse by seeing relatable examples. The Ideas tab helps users overcome the difficulty of writing a first prompt, while the team is moving toward tiered onboarding for early adopters and later users with less familiarity with agents.

takeaways.heading: Product design choices
takeaways.detail: Muse deliberately used chat bubbles rather than the large-canvas format common among AI products, aiming to make interaction feel like messaging a personal entity. The team initially favored one main chat because the agent retained long-running context, then added side chats after strong employee demand.

takeaways.heading: Let engineers cook
takeaways.detail: The team’s “let them cook” culture gave engineers and designers room to pursue small ideas and return with working prototypes. Mona said this autonomy was especially valuable with a small, talent-dense team whose members had strong product judgment.

takeaways.heading: Learning through failure
takeaways.detail: When two Muses were allowed to converse, they accidentally exposed private medical information and later got into a passive-aggressive argument. These experiments revealed that discretion and agent-to-agent communication were much harder problems than the team had initially considered.

takeaways.heading: The changing PM role
takeaways.detail: Mona believes AI has transformed product management through rapid prototyping, easier internal-tool creation, and more concrete discussions. She said product taste, customer empathy, and the ability to maintain a high quality bar matter increasingly because AI makes it easy to build and deploy mediocre products.

takeaways.heading: Future direction
takeaways.detail: Mona expects Muse to become more ambient, appearing in glasses, charm devices, and other interfaces rather than remaining trapped in an app. She also hopes agents can become more autonomous, affordable, and broadly useful for health, time savings, financial security, and starting new businesses or side hustles.
